issues.legal_issue: A claim of undue influence must be specifically pleaded and cannot be supplied by the court from vague allegations or an opposing party’s pleading.
material_facts: The suit was pleaded as a challenge to a transfer obtained by fraud and misrepresentation, alongside general assertions that the transferor was old, simple, and confident in the transferee.
The plaint did not give particulars showing how the transferee could dominate the transferor’s will, how that influence was exercised, or why it was undue.
The opposing pleading described a close, affectionate relationship but did not admit that the transferee could dominate the transferor’s will.
Undue influence was not specifically put in issue or pursued at trial or in the first appeal.
issues.conclusion: The claim of undue influence was not adequately pleaded, and the High Court could not construct that claim from the opposing party’s pleading or general allegations in the plaint.
issues.legal_principle: Under Order 6, Rules 2 and 4 of the Code of Civil Procedure, undue influence, fraud, and misrepresentation are distinct legal grounds that must be separately pleaded with specificity, particularity, and precision. A party must succeed on the case alleged and proved, consistently with the maxim secundum allegata et probata, and cannot be given a new case beyond the pleadings and issues.

predicates.undue_influence_claim: A claimant seeks to avoid a transaction on the ground that the other party exercised undue influence.
predicates.vague_allegations_without_particulars: The claimant alleges general dependence, age, confidence, or a close relationship without stating how the other party could dominate the claimant’s will or how undue influence was exercised.
predicates.opposing_pleading_describes_relationship: The opposing party describes a close or affectionate relationship but does not admit being in a position to dominate the claimant’s will.

issues.definition: When a claimant alleging undue influence offers only general allegations and the opposing party’s description of the relationship does not admit dominance, the court cannot supply an unpleaded undue-influence case.

issues.legal_issue: Undue influence is not established, and the burden does not shift to the beneficiary, unless the claimant first proves that the beneficiary could dominate the claimant’s will and that the transaction was unconscionable.
material_facts: The first appellate court found that the transferee was not in a position to dominate the transferor’s will and had not exercised undue influence.
The transferor was old but was physically fit, and there was no evidence that age or another cause impaired his mental capacity to understand the deed.

The deed writer testified that the deed was prepared on the transferor’s instructions, read to him, accepted by him as correct, and then thumbmarked by him; an attesting witness corroborated that account.

The first appellate court found the deed writer and attesting witness independent and credible, and found that the transferor executed the deed voluntarily after understanding its contents and effect.
issues.conclusion: The claimant failed to prove the beneficiary’s ability to dominate the claimant’s will, so undue influence was not established and the burden did not shift to the beneficiary.
issues.legal_principle: Section 16 of the Indian Contract Act, 1872, requires the court to consider in sequence whether the beneficiary could dominate the donor’s will, whether that position was used to obtain an unfair advantage, and, if the transaction is unconscionable, whether the burden shifts to the beneficiary to show that the transaction was not induced by undue influence. The burden shifts only when the claimant proves both dominance and an unconscionable transaction. The Court relied on Subhas Chandra v. Gana Prasad, which approved the stages stated in Raghunath Prasad v. Sarju Prasad, and on Poosathurai v. Kappanna Chettiar for the requirement that more than mere influence must be shown to establish undue influence.

predicates.undue_influence_claim: A claimant seeks to set aside a transaction on the ground that the beneficiary exercised undue influence.
predicates.beneficiary_dominance_not_proved: The evidence does not establish that the beneficiary was in a position to dominate the other party’s will.

issues.definition: If a claimant challenges a transaction for undue influence but does not prove that the beneficiary could dominate the claimant’s will, undue influence is not established.

issues.legal_issue: A High Court cannot reopen a fairly reached finding of fact in a second appeal unless the finding is affected by a legal or procedural defect of the kind that permits second-appellate interference.
material_facts: The first appellate court, acting as the final court of fact after remand, found that the transferee was not in a position to dominate the transferor’s will and that the deed was not induced by undue influence.
The High Court reversed that finding in a second appeal without identifying an illegality, omission, error, or defect that would permit interference with the factual finding.
issues.conclusion: The High Court had no jurisdiction to interfere with the first appellate court’s finding of fact in the second appeal.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 100 and 101 of the Code of Civil Procedure limit a second appeal to an error of law or procedure, not merely an error of fact. Under Section 103, the High Court may determine an issue of fact only in the specified circumstances where the lower appellate court did not determine it or determined it wrongly because of a defect of the kind referred to in Section 100(1). A finding on whether a party could dominate another’s will and procured a deed by undue influence is a finding of fact. The Court referred to Mst. Durga Chaudhrani v. Jawahar Singh, Satgur Prasad v. Har Narain Das, and Ladli Parshad Jaiswal v. The Karnal Distillery Co. Ltd.

predicates.second_appeal: The proceeding before the High Court is a second appeal from a lower appellate decision.
predicates.lower_appellate_court_fairly_determined_: The lower appellate court determined the relevant factual issue fairly and in accordance with the prescribed procedure.
predicates.no_qualifying_legal_or_procedural_defect: The factual determination is not affected by an illegality, omission, error, or defect that permits second-appellate interference.

issues.definition: When a lower appellate court has fairly determined a fact and no qualifying legal or procedural defect is present, the High Court cannot reopen that finding in a second appeal.
